These eighteen are the old districts, each named for its capital town,
so every hook is really a town name. Three layers again, as in Spain:
pre-Roman (Braga's Bracari, Évora, Beja), Latin (Portus Cale, Castelo
Branco, Vila Real) and Arabic in the south (Faro, the Algarve, Alcácer).
Ids drop the accents and the cedilla, so Bragança is 'braganca'.
viana-do-castelo: "Viana by the castle" — Viana is an old name of uncertain root, and do Castelo was added to tell it from two other Vianas.
The Lima river here was taken by the Romans for the Lethe, the river of forgetting; a general had to cross first and shout back the names of his men to prove it was safe.
Its gold filigree jewellery is the finest in the country, and the costume worn with it is the image of Portuguese folk dress.
braga: From the Bracari, a Celtic people; Rome made it Bracara Augusta and it became the religious capital of the country.
Its archbishops outranked Lisbon's for centuries, and the saying goes that Braga prays while Porto works.
Bom Jesus do Monte above the town climbs a baroque staircase of nearly six hundred steps, and a water-counterweight funicular from 1882 still hauls those who decline.
vila-real: "Royal town", founded by King Dinis in 1289 — a plain name for a plain royal foundation.
The Douro valley below it is the oldest demarcated wine region in the world, set out in 1756.
Its terraces were cut into schist by hand over three centuries, and are a UNESCO site for it.
braganca: An old, probably Celtic name; the dukes of Bragança took it, and in 1640 became the royal house that ruled Portugal until 1910.
The remotest district, up against Spain, and its people speak Mirandese — a separate language, official since 1999, with about 15,000 speakers.
Montesinho park here is one of the last places in Iberia with wolves.
porto: From Portus Cale, the Roman harbour at the Douro mouth — the name of the town became the name of the country.
Port wine is named for it, though the wine is grown 100 km upriver and only aged in Vila Nova de Gaia across the water.
Its Luís I bridge was built in 1886 by a partner of Gustave Eiffel, and the Lello bookshop below it is claimed as an inspiration for Hogwarts.
viseu: Probably from Latin visum, a view or lookout, for the hill the town stands on.
Viriathus, the shepherd who led the Lusitanians against Rome for eight years, is said to have come from here.
The Dão around it makes some of Portugal's most respected red wine, from granite soils at altitude.
guarda: Simply "the guard" — a frontier watch post against Castile, founded in 1199.
The highest city in Portugal at 1,056 m, and the coldest: the local rhyme calls it rich, healthy, cold and strong.
The Serra da Estrela beside it holds the country's highest mainland point and its only ski slopes.
aveiro: Most likely from Latin aviarium, a place of birds, for the lagoon and its waterfowl.
Called the Portuguese Venice for the canals its moliceiro boats work, built to gather seaweed for fertiliser.
Its ovos moles — egg yolk and sugar in a wafer shell — were invented by nuns and now carry a protected designation.
coimbra: From Conimbriga, a Celtic hill fort nearby; briga means a fortified place, the same element as in many Iberian names.
Its university, founded in 1290, is one of the oldest in continuous operation anywhere, and its baroque library is kept free of insects by a colony of bats.
The capital of Portugal for over a century in the Middle Ages, before Lisbon took over.
castelo-branco: "White castle", for the Templar stronghold on the hill.
Its embroidered silk bedspreads have been made to the same designs since the 1600s.
The Tejo Internacional park on its Spanish border is one of the best places in Europe for vultures and Bonelli's eagles.
leiria: Probably from Latin legionarium, ground belonging to a legion, or from leira, a strip of tilled land.
The pine forest of Leiria was planted by King Dinis around 1300 to hold back the dunes — and it built the ships of the Discoveries.
Fátima is in this district, and the 1917 apparitions there draw millions of pilgrims a year.
santarem: From Santa Iria, a nun martyred here — Shantarin under the Moors, worn down to Santarém.
The Tejo's floodplain around it is the country's bull-breeding and horse country, and its fair is Portugal's oldest.
Almeirim nearby is where the stone soup story is set, and every restaurant serves it.
portalegre: "Cheerful gate" or "high gate" — portus alacer, a pass through the hills on the Spanish road.
Its tapestry workshop developed a stitch of its own and wove for Picasso, Le Corbusier and Vieira da Silva.
Marvão on its border is a village inside a wall on a crag, and from it you can see most of the Alentejo.
lisboa: The oldest layer of all: probably Phoenician Alis Ubbo, "safe harbour", though the Romans preferred a legend about Ulysses founding it.
The 1755 earthquake, fire and tsunami killed tens of thousands and led to the first scientific study of an earthquake anywhere.
Its Belém tower and Jerónimos monastery were paid for with a 5% tax on the spices coming back from India.
evora: Pre-Roman, possibly from Celtic ebora, "of the yews"; Rome called it Liberalitas Julia.
Its Roman temple still stands in the middle of the town because it was walled up and used as a butcher's shop for centuries.
The Almendres stone circle outside it is about 2,000 years older than Stonehenge.
setubal: Uncertain: possibly from Cetobriga, a Roman fish-salting town, with briga again the fortified place.
Its estuary holds a resident pod of bottlenose dolphins, one of very few in Europe.
The Arrábida hills beside it drop straight into the sea, and the moscatel grown on them is fortified like port.
beja: From Pax Julia, the peace Caesar made with the Lusitanians — Pax became Baja under the Moors and then Beja.
The flattest and hottest part of Portugal, wheat and cork as far as the horizon, and 47 °C has been recorded here.
Alqueva on its edge is the largest artificial lake in western Europe, and the sky above it is a certified dark-sky reserve.
faro: From Arabic Ḥārūn, a local lord's name — and the Algarve around it is al-gharb, "the west", the western edge of Moorish Iberia.
The last part of Portugal to be taken from the Moors, in 1249, which is why its towns are the most Arab in layout.
The Ria Formosa lagoon in front of it is a chain of barrier islands that shifts, and it produces most of Portugal's clams.
